The author is using **these with these** as a common expression of his culture to mean that the Israelite leaders drew lots from a collection that included the names of the clans of the descendants of both Elezar and Ithamar. The idea is that the lots were drawn impartially, without giving an advantage to the descendants of either man. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [selecting from the descendants of both men together] or [impartially]

The expression **and was taken, was taken** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed that a scribe may have written the last consonant of a word incorrectly. With a different consonant, this would say “and one was taken,” which seems to fit the meaning of this passage better. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [One house of a father was taken for Eleazar, and one was taken for Ithamar]
בֵּֽית־אָ֣ב אֶחָ֗ד אָחֻז֙ לְ⁠אֶלְעָזָ֔ר וְ⁠אָחֻ֥ז ׀ אָחֻ֖ז לְ⁠אִיתָמָֽר

Since the author says in verse 5 that “they divided them by lots, these with these,” he does not seem to mean here that the officials alternately drew lots to give assignments to clans descended from Eleazar and clans descended from Ithamar. (That procedure would only have worked for eight rounds, after which eight clans from Eleazar would have remained without counterparts from Ithamar.) Instead, the author seems to be using an expression equivalent to “these with these”: **one … for Eleazar, and one … for Ithamar**. The idea seems to be that the assignment that went with a lot did not depend on which ancestor a clan had. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The assignment that went with the lot did not depend on whether Eleazar or Ithamar was the ancestor of the clan whose name was drawn]

nt: See how you translated the same expression in [23:32](../23/32.md). Alternate translation: [their kinsmen]

The author is referring to all of these Levite clans by naming two extremes, those descended from **fathers of the head** and those descended from a **youngest brother**. It seems that the expression **fathers of the head** is equivalent to **heads of fathers**, that is, heads of father’s houses or clans, and that it indicates an eldest brother who was a family leader. The idea is that the leaders did not take birth order, and thus family rank, into consideration in these assignments. This is another description of an impartial process, likes the ones in verses 5 and 6. The UST models one way to express this meaning in plain language.

The author is not referring to a specific **youngest brother**. He means the youngest brothers in all of the clans he has listed. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [their youngest brothers]
